## field splitting

| case | dash | bash | bash-as-sh | ksh93 | zsh |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `split/unquoted-param` | `[a][b]` | `[a][b]` | `[a][b]` | `[a][b]` | `[a b]` |
| `split/quoted-param` | `[a b]` | `[a b]` | `[a b]` | `[a b]` | `[a b]` |
| `split/cmdsub-unquoted` | `n=2` | `n=2` | `n=2` | `n=2` | `n=2` |
| `split/param-braced` | `n=2` | `n=2` | `n=2` | `n=2` | `n=1` |
| `split/empty-value` | `n=0` | `n=0` | `n=0` | `n=0` | `n=0` |
| `split/empty-value-quoted` | `n=1` | `n=1` | `n=1` | `n=1` | `n=1` |
| `split/unset-value` | `n=0` | `n=0` | `n=0` | `n=0` | `n=0` |

- `split/unquoted-param` — the base case: an unquoted parameter expansion is split
  ```sh
  x="a b"; set -- $x; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```
- `split/quoted-param` — quoting suppresses splitting; without this the base case proves nothing
  ```sh
  x="a b"; set -- "$x"; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```
- `split/cmdsub-unquoted` — zsh does not split parameter expansions but does split this — the axis is narrower than 'word splitting'
  ```sh
  set -- $(printf "a b"); echo "n=$#"
  ```
- `split/param-braced` — braces are not quoting; ${x} splits wherever $x does
  ```sh
  x="a b"; set -- ${x}; echo "n=$#"
  ```
- `split/empty-value` — an unquoted empty expansion produces no field at all
  ```sh
  x=""; set -- $x; echo "n=$#"
  ```
- `split/empty-value-quoted` — quoted, the same value produces one empty field — the pair is the point
  ```sh
  x=""; set -- "$x"; echo "n=$#"
  ```
- `split/unset-value` — unset behaves as empty here, rather than as an error
  ```sh
  unset u; set -- $u; echo "n=$#"
  ```

## IFS

| case | dash | bash | bash-as-sh | ksh93 | zsh |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ifs/default-runs-collapse` | `[a][b][c]` | `[a][b][c]` | `[a][b][c]` | `[a][b][c]` | `[a b   c]` |
| `ifs/default-edges-stripped` | `[a][b]` | `[a][b]` | `[a][b]` | `[a][b]` | `[  a  b  ]` |
| `ifs/nonws-separates` | `[a][b][c]` | `[a][b][c]` | `[a][b][c]` | `[a][b][c]` | `[a:b:c]` |
| `ifs/nonws-adjacent-empty-field` | `[a][][b]` | `[a][][b]` | `[a][][b]` | `[a][][b]` | `[a::b]` |
| `ifs/nonws-leading` | `[][a]` | `[][a]` | `[][a]` | `[][a]` | `[:a]` |
| `ifs/nonws-trailing` | `[a]` | `[a]` | `[a]` | `[a]` | `[a:]` |
| `ifs/nonws-only-delimiters` | `n=2` | `n=2` | `n=2` | `n=2` | `n=1` |
| `ifs/mixed-ws-around-nonws` | `[a][b]` | `[a][b]` | `[a][b]` | `[a][b]` | `[a : b]` |
| `ifs/mixed-adjacent-nonws` | `[a][][b]` | `[a][][b]` | `[a][][b]` | `[a][][b]` | `[a::b]` |
| `ifs/empty-disables-splitting` | `[a b]` | `[a b]` | `[a b]` | `[a b]` | `[a b]` |
| `ifs/unset-is-default` | `[a][b]` | `[a][b]` | `[a][b]` | `[a][b]` | `[a b]` |

- `ifs/default-runs-collapse` — a run of IFS whitespace is one delimiter
  ```sh
  x="a b   c"; set -- $x; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```
- `ifs/default-edges-stripped` — leading and trailing IFS whitespace is discarded entirely
  ```sh
  x="  a  b  "; set -- $x; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```
- `ifs/nonws-separates` — each non-whitespace IFS character delimits
  ```sh
  IFS=:; x="a:b:c"; set -- $x; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```
- `ifs/nonws-adjacent-empty-field` — adjacent non-whitespace delimiters produce an empty field, unlike whitespace
  ```sh
  IFS=:; x="a::b"; set -- $x; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```
- `ifs/nonws-leading` — half of the leading/trailing asymmetry: a leading delimiter makes an empty field
  ```sh
  IFS=:; x=":a"; set -- $x; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```
- `ifs/nonws-trailing` — the other half: a trailing delimiter does not. A symmetric implementation fails here
  ```sh
  IFS=:; x="a:"; set -- $x; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```
- `ifs/nonws-only-delimiters` — pins the asymmetry as a count rather than as a rendering
  ```sh
  IFS=:; x="::"; set -- $x; echo "n=$#"
  ```
- `ifs/mixed-ws-around-nonws` — whitespace around a non-whitespace delimiter joins it into one delimiter
  ```sh
  IFS=" :"; x="a : b"; set -- $x; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```
- `ifs/mixed-adjacent-nonws` — mixing does not disable the empty-field rule
  ```sh
  IFS=" :"; x="a::b"; set -- $x; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```
- `ifs/empty-disables-splitting` — an empty IFS disables the stage; it does not mean 'split on nothing'
  ```sh
  IFS=; x="a b"; set -- $x; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```
- `ifs/unset-is-default` — unset is not the same state as empty, and restores the default
  ```sh
  unset IFS; x="a b"; set -- $x; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```

## special parameters

| case | dash | bash | bash-as-sh | ksh93 | zsh |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `params/at-quoted-keeps-fields` | `[a b][c]` | `[a b][c]` | `[a b][c]` | `[a b][c]` | `[a b][c]` |
| `params/star-quoted-joins` | `[a b]` | `[a b]` | `[a b]` | `[a b]` | `[a b]` |
| `params/star-joins-with-ifs` | `[a:b]` | `[a:b]` | `[a:b]` | `[a:b]` | `[a:b]` |
| `params/at-empty-is-zero-fields` | `n=0` | `n=0` | `n=0` | `n=0` | `n=0` |
| `params/star-empty-is-one-field` | `n=1` | `n=1` | `n=1` | `n=1` | `n=1` |

- `params/at-quoted-keeps-fields` — "$@" is one field per parameter, each keeping its spaces
  ```sh
  set -- "a b" c; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```
- `params/star-quoted-joins` — "$*" joins into a single field
  ```sh
  set -- a b; printf "[%s]" "$*"
  ```
- `params/star-joins-with-ifs` — the joiner is IFS's first character, not a space
  ```sh
  set -- a b; IFS=:; printf "[%s]" "$*"
  ```
- `params/at-empty-is-zero-fields` — "$@" with no parameters yields zero fields — why set -- "$@" is safe
  ```sh
  set --; set -- "$@"; echo "n=$#"
  ```
- `params/star-empty-is-one-field` — "$*" yields one empty field instead — why set -- "$*" is not safe
  ```sh
  set --; set -- "$*"; echo "n=$#"
  ```

## expansion

| case | dash | bash | bash-as-sh | ksh93 | zsh |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `expand/results-not-rescanned-quote` | `[a"b]` | `[a"b]` | `[a"b]` | `[a"b]` | `[a"b]` |
| `expand/results-not-rescanned-dollar` | `$HOME` | `$HOME` | `$HOME` | `$HOME` | `$HOME` |
| `expand/results-not-rescanned-semicolon` | `[a;b]` | `[a;b]` | `[a;b]` | `[a;b]` | `[a;b]` |
| `expand/glob-applies-to-expansion` | `[etc]` | `[etc]` | `[etc]` | `[etc]` | `[et*]` |
| `expand/glob-not-applied-when-quoted` | `[et*]` | `[et*]` | `[et*]` | `[et*]` | `[et*]` |
| `expand/glob-literal-pattern` | `[etc]` | `[etc]` | `[etc]` | `[etc]` | `[etc]` |
| `expand/glob-no-match` | `/zzz_no_such*` | `/zzz_no_such*` | `/zzz_no_such*` | `/zzz_no_such*` | `<shell>:1: no matches found: /zzz_no_such*` *(status 1)* |
| `expand/brace` | `{1..3}` | `1 2 3` | `1 2 3` | `1 2 3` | `1 2 3` |
| `expand/brace-before-param` | `{1,2}` | `1 2` | `1 2` | `1 2` | `1 2` |
| `expand/tilde-unquoted` | `abs` | `abs` | `abs` | `abs` | `abs` |
| `expand/tilde-quoted` | `literal` | `literal` | `literal` | `literal` | `literal` |
| `expand/tilde-in-assignment` | `abs` | `abs` | `abs` | `abs` | `abs` |

- `expand/results-not-rescanned-quote` — a quote in expanded text is a literal quote
  ```sh
  x="a\"b"; set -- $x; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```
- `expand/results-not-rescanned-dollar` — expansion does not recurse; this is why eval exists
  ```sh
  x="\$HOME"; echo "$x"
  ```
- `expand/results-not-rescanned-semicolon` — an operator in expanded text is data, not syntax
  ```sh
  x="a;b"; set -- $x; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```
- `expand/glob-applies-to-expansion` — globbing runs after splitting, so an expansion result is matched — except in zsh
  ```sh
  cd /; x="et*"; set -- $x; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```
- `expand/glob-not-applied-when-quoted` — quoting the expansion suppresses the match; the pair isolates the cause
  ```sh
  cd /; x="et*"; set -- "$x"; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```
- `expand/glob-literal-pattern` — a literal pattern is matched even in zsh — separating that from expansion results
  ```sh
  cd /; set -- et*; printf "[%s]" "$@"
  ```
- `expand/glob-no-match` — an unmatched pattern passes through, except in zsh where it is an error
  ```sh
  echo /zzz_no_such*
  ```
- `expand/brace` — brace expansion is absent from dash
  ```sh
  echo {1..3}
  ```
- `expand/brace-before-param` — braces resolve before parameter expansion, so variable ranges cannot work
  ```sh
  a=1; echo {$a,2}
  ```
- `expand/tilde-unquoted` — an unquoted leading tilde expands
  ```sh
  case $(echo ~) in /*) echo abs;; *) echo literal;; esac
  ```
- `expand/tilde-quoted` — quoting suppresses it
  ```sh
  case "$(echo "~")" in /*) echo abs;; *) echo literal;; esac
  ```
- `expand/tilde-in-assignment` — assignment values are a tilde context, which is why PATH=~/bin works
  ```sh
  x=~; case $x in /*) echo abs;; *) echo literal;; esac
  ```

## semantics axes

| case | dash | bash | bash-as-sh | ksh93 | zsh |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `axis/array-base` | `<shell>: 1: Syntax error: "(" unexpected` *(status 2)* | `y` | `y` | `y` | `x` |
| `axis/echo-backslash` | `expanded` | `literal` | `expanded` | `literal` | `expanded` |
| `axis/pipeline-last-element` | `[]` | `[]` | `[]` | `[x]` | `[x]` |
| `axis/dollar-zero-in-function` | `<shell>` | `<shell>` | `<shell>` | `<shell>` | `f` |
| `axis/local-builtin` | `1` | `1` | `1` | `<shell>: local: not found` | `1` |
| `axis/shift-past-end` | `<shell>: 1: shift: can't shift that many` *(status 2)* | `survived` | `survived` | `<shell>: shift: 5: bad number` *(status 1)* | `<shell>:shift:1: shift count must be <= $#~survived` |
| `axis/readonly-reassign` | `<script>: 2: r: is read only` *(status 2)* | `<script>: line 2: r: readonly variable~survived` | `<script>: line 2: r: readonly variable` *(status 1)* | `<script>: line 2: r: is read only` *(status 1)* | `<script>:2: read-only variable: r` *(status 1)* |

- `axis/array-base` — zsh indexes arrays from 1; dash has no arrays at all
  ```sh
  a=(x y); echo "${a[1]}"
  ```
- `axis/echo-backslash` — dash and zsh expand escapes in echo; bash and ksh do not — a grouping no ladder predicts
  ```sh
  if [ "$(echo 'a\tb')" = 'a\tb' ]; then echo literal; else echo expanded; fi
  ```
- `axis/pipeline-last-element` — ksh and zsh run the last pipeline element in the current shell; dash and bash use a subshell
  ```sh
  echo x | read v; echo "[$v]"
  ```
- `axis/dollar-zero-in-function` — zsh reports the function name where the others report the shell
  ```sh
  f() { echo "$0"; }; f
  ```
- `axis/local-builtin` — ksh93 is the only panel member without local, which is why it is not a compatibility target
  ```sh
  f() { local v=1; echo "$v"; }; f
  ```
- `axis/shift-past-end` — fatal in dash and ksh, survivable in bash and zsh
  ```sh
  shift 5; echo survived
  ```
- `axis/readonly-reassign` — must be a plain assignment in a script: adding a redirect makes it a command and reverses the answer
  ```sh
  readonly r=1
  r=2
  echo survived
  ```
